a: Manasseh
t: The prayer Chronicles mentions but does not give
p: 2 Chronicles 33 says Manasseh prayed in captivity and that his prayer was written down. It never gives the words.
b: Manasseh was king of Judah for fifty-five years (2 Kings 21:1). Kings tells only of his evil and never of a change of heart: "Manasseh shed innocent blood, a great deal of it" (2 Kings 21:16). Chronicles adds a turn. Assyrian officers "bound him in bronze fetters and led him off to Babylon"; there "he humbled himself deeply," prayed, and God "heard his pleading and brought him back to Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). Twice it says the prayer was written in the records (2 Chronicles 33:18–19), but it does not copy it. This prayer fills that gap. It names no place, no king of Assyria and no event, so it can be read as anyone's prayer, but its heading and its iron chain (1:10) point to the scene in Chronicles.

a: Lord Almighty
p: The Greek is Kyrie pantokrator, "Lord, ruler of all." It is rendered as in Judith and the other Greek books.
b: Pantokratōr means "the one who holds power over everything." The site renders the title "the Lord Almighty" in the Greek books outside the Hebrew Bible, so the Greek pantokratōr is rendered here as it is in Judith. The prayer is in Greek and has no divine name, so "Lord" here is never printed "the LORD" (see the note on the term at Tobit and Judith). Verses 1–7 are one long address: the prayer piles up who God is before it says a word about the one praying.

a: the righteous who came from them
p: The prayer sets the righteous fathers against the sinner who prays. Genesis is less tidy.
b: The prayer calls Abraham, Isaac and Jacob "righteous" and says in 1:8 that they "had not sinned against you." That is a way of speaking, to make the contrast with the king as sharp as it can be. Genesis does call Abraham's trust righteousness (Genesis 15:6), but it also shows him passing off his wife as his sister (Genesis 12:11–13) and Jacob deceiving his father (Genesis 27:18–24). Here the prayer goes beyond the Bible's own picture. Readers who pray it in church take the line as praise of the fathers' faith, not as a claim that they never did wrong.

a: with all their array
p: The Greek kosmos first meant order or adornment, the well-arranged finery of a thing.
b: Kosmos later came to mean "the world," but its older sense is "order" or "decoration": what makes something beautiful and well-arranged. Heaven and earth were made "with all their kosmos," all that fills and furnishes them, stars, seas, creatures. The idea is close to the close of the creation story, "the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their crowded host" (Genesis 2:1).
orig: σὺν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ αὐτῶν (syn panti tō kosmō autōn)

a: You put the sea in fetters
t: The chained sea and the chained king
p: The Greek verb means to shackle someone's feet. The God who puts the sea in irons hears a man in irons.
b: Pedaō is the word for putting a prisoner's feet in fetters. In the Bible the sea is the great unruly power that God holds back by command: "Up to here you may come, but not one step more" (Job 38:11; compare Jeremiah 5:22; Psalm 104:9). The abyss, the deep waters under the world, is "shut" and "sealed," as the angel in Revelation shuts and seals the abyss over the dragon (Revelation 20:3). The prayer opens with God binding the wildest things in creation; by 1:10 the one praying is himself the one in chains, and in 1:13 he begs God to let him go.
orig: ὁ πεδήσας τὴν θάλασσαν (ho pedēsas tēn thalassan)

a: sealed it with your fearsome and glorious name
p: A seal marks ownership and keeps a thing shut. Here the seal on the abyss is God's own name.
b: In the ancient world a seal pressed into clay or wax closed a jar, a door or a document, and only the owner could break it. To seal the abyss "with your name" is to say the deep belongs to God and stays shut by his authority. The "name" stands for God himself as he has made himself known (compare "In Jerusalem my name will be forever," 2 Chronicles 33:4, the very house Manasseh filled with altars). "Fearsome" and "glorious" join the two sides the prayer goes on to describe: God is terrible to sinners (1:5) and boundless in mercy (1:6).

a: no one can stand against your anger
p: "Unbearable" and "irresistible" are strong words, and the prayer's Greek is formal and careful.
b: The Greek says the splendor is astektos, "not to be borne," and the anger anypostatos, "not to be withstood." The Plain English Translation turns both into "no one can" sentences so that an 8th-grade reader feels their force. Whether the prayer was first written in Greek or Hebrew is disputed (the Jewish Encyclopedia names F. C. Porter and Swete for Greek, Ewald and Budde, 1892, for Hebrew; the introduction in Charles's Apocrypha calls Greek "most probable"; Bruce Metzger called the question disputed; see the book page).

a: slow to anger and great in mercy
p: Verse 7 echoes the words God speaks to Moses about himself, the Bible's most repeated description of God.
b: When God passes before Moses he calls out: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). Joel and Jonah repeat it with one more line: "slow to anger and great in loyal love, and he changes his mind about the harm" (Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). The prayer follows the Joel and Jonah form, ending with God changing his mind (see the next note). Jonah was angry that God forgave Nineveh; the king who prays here stakes everything on the same words.

a: you change your mind
p: The Greek verb is the one for "repent" in 1:8 and 1:13. The site renders God's "repenting" as "change your mind."
b:
Literally God is "repenting over the evils of human beings." The verb metanoeō is the same root as "repentance" (metanoia) in 1:8 and "those who repent" in 1:13. The prayer plays on it: God, who "repents" of harm, has made "repentance" a road for sinners. English "repent" sounds like regret for sin, which God has none of, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording for the same idea in Joel 2:13, "he changes his mind about the harm" (compare Jeremiah 18:8; Jonah 3:10).

"The evils of human beings" can mean the harm that falls on people (as in Joel and Jonah, where God holds back a disaster) or the evil people do. The Plain English Translation takes the first, which fits the formula of verse 7; the KJV Apocrypha keeps the ambiguity ("repentest of the evils of men").
orig: μετανοῶν ἐπὶ κακίαις ἀνθρώπων (metanoōn epi kakiais anthrōpōn)

a: did not set repentance for the righteous
p: Jesus says almost the same thing in Luke: he came "to call sinners to repentance," not the righteous.
b:
The thought is bold: repentance is not a burden laid on the good but a gift made for the bad. Luke uses the same Greek words, "righteous" (dikaioi), "sinners" and "repentance": "I have not come to call righteous people. I have come to call sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32), and "there will be more joy there over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance" (Luke 15:7). There is no sign that either text knows the other. They show the same Jewish conviction about God's mercy toward the lost.

The Greek verb "set" (ethou, "you placed, appointed") makes repentance something God has arranged, not something the sinner invents.
orig: οὐκ ἔθου μετάνοιαν δικαίοις (ouk ethou metanoian dikaiois)

a: me, the sinner
p: The Greek is the same three words as the tax collector's prayer in Luke 18:13.
b: The Greek ends emoi tō hamartōlō, "to me, the sinner." The tax collector in Jesus' parable prays, "God, be gracious to me, the sinner" (Luke 18:13), in Greek moi tō hamartōlō. In both the article "the" matters: not "a sinner" among others, but the one who stands before God as nothing but a sinner. The tax collector also "would not even raise his eyes toward heaven," much as the king says he is not fit to look up (1:9). Orthodox worship reads the prayer at Great Compline in Lent (see the chapter page).

a: beyond the count of the sand of the sea
t: The sand of the sea, turned around
p: God promised Abraham offspring like the sand of the sea. The king uses the same picture to count his sins.
b: "Make your offspring as many as the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17; compare Genesis 32:12). The prayer has just named Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (1:8). Their blessing was a number too great to count; the king's sins are a number too great to count. He is the fathers' offspring, but what he has multiplied is wrongdoing ("my lawless deeds have piled up").

a: A heavy iron chain bends me low
p: Chronicles says bronze fetters; the prayer says one heavy iron bond. Later retellings make the iron the center of the story.
b:
In the site's 2 Chronicles the Assyrians "bound him in bronze fetters" (2 Chronicles 33:11). The prayer speaks of a single "bond" "of iron" (in the Greek, pollō desmō sidērou, "a heavy bond of iron"; both nouns and the adjective in the singular), where Chronicles has fetters in the plural. The Apostolic Constitutions (book 2, section 22) retell the story so that Manasseh is bound both "in fetters of brass" and "shackled with iron all over," and after his prayer "a flame of fire" surrounds him and the iron shackles fall off. The Jewish Encyclopedia reports a similar legend from the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 10:2): Manasseh was shut inside an iron mule over a fire, prayed in vain to his idols, and was saved when he called on the God of his fathers.

The iron also explains the posture: bent over by the weight, he cannot lift his head.

a: abhorrent things
t: Abhorrent things and things God loathes
p: Two Greek Bible words for idols. They sum up everything Kings and Chronicles say Manasseh built.
b: Bdelygmata, "abhorrent things," is the word Kings uses for the nations' practices Manasseh copied ("the abhorrent ways of the nations," 2 Kings 21:2). Prosochthismata, "things that rouse loathing," is a Greek Bible word for idols. The list in Kings and Chronicles is long: altars for the Baals, an Asherah pole, altars to the army of the heavens inside the LORD's house, his sons passed through the fire, a carved image in God's house (2 Chronicles 33:3–7). The prayer confesses all of it in two lines and names none of it.
orig: στήσας βδελύγματα καὶ πληθύνας προσοχθίσματα (stēsas bdelygmata kai plēthynas prosochthismata)

a: I bend my heart's knee
p: A man bent double by chains cannot kneel. So he kneels inside. The picture is the prayer's most famous line.
b:
Kneeling was a posture of prayer (Solomon "had been down on his knees, with his palms spread toward the heavens," 1 Kings 8:54). The Greek klinō gony kardias, "I bend the knee of the heart," moves the gesture inward: what counts is the humbled heart, "a heart broken and crushed" (Psalm 51:17). The same picture appears in 1 Clement, a letter of the church in Rome to Corinth near the end of the first century AD, which urges the leaders of a revolt to submit, "bending the knees of your hearts" (1 Clement 57:1). Whether Clement knew this prayer or both drew on a common way of speaking cannot be shown.

The Greek has "the knee of the heart"; one manuscript (T, the Zurich Psalter) adds "my," which English needs anyway.

a: I have sinned, Lord, I have sinned
p: The doubled "I have sinned" and "I myself know" sound like David's confession in Psalm 51.
b: "I myself know my rebellious acts; my sin stands before me all the time" (Psalm 51:3). The Greek here has the same emphatic "I" (egō ginōskō). The doubling, "I have sinned ... I have sinned," is the language of confession found in Daniel's prayer ("We have sinned and gone wrong," Daniel 9:5) and in the son who comes home in Jesus' parable ("Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight," Luke 15:18).

a: let me go free, Lord, let me go free
p: The Greek verb means to loosen. It is the root of "relief" in 1:10 and can also mean forgive.
b: Anes moi, from aniēmi, "loosen, let go," picks up 1:10, where the king has "no relief" (anesis, a loosening). To a man in chains "let me go" is a plea to be unchained; to a man weighed down by sin it is a plea to be forgiven. The KJV Apocrypha chose the second sense ("forgive me, O Lord, forgive me"). The Plain English Translation keeps the double sense, since the prayer moves from chains to sin and back.
orig: ἄνες μοι, Κύριε, ἄνες μοι (anes moi, Kyrie, anes moi)

a: the lowest parts of the earth
p: A Bible phrase for the world of the dead, deep below the ground.
b: The same words stand in Psalm 63:9 ("those who seek my life ... will enter the lowest parts of the earth") and, of the womb's hidden place, in Psalm 139:15; Ephesians 4:9 says Christ "came down into the lower parts of the earth." Here the king asks not to be condemned to the depth of death, the opposite of the "height of heaven" he dares not look at (1:9).
orig: ἐν τοῖς κατωτάτοις τῆς γῆς (en tois katōtatois tēs gēs)

a: the God of those who repent
p: God is called "the God of Abraham" in 1:1. Now he is "the God of those who repent."
b:
The prayer begins with "God of our fathers" (1:1) and "God of the righteous" (1:8) and ends with a new title, "God of those who repent." The penitent are now a people God belongs to, as the fathers were. The Jewish Encyclopedia saw in this stress on God as the God of the penitent, with the patriarchs as models, a mark of later Judaism, and judged the author "evidently a Jew."

Christians have read the line as the gospel in short: Orthodox worship places it at Great Compline, Article VI of the Church of England lists the prayer among the books read "for example of life," and Lutheran Bibles kept it (see the book page). For Jewish tradition, the Mishnah records that Rabbi Judah gave Manasseh a share in the world to come because he repented, while the other sages said God restored his kingdom but not that share (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2).

a: You will save me, though I am unworthy
p: The prayer asks for nothing on the ground of the king's worth. Here it agrees fully with the Bible.
b: The ground of the plea is God's mercy alone: "as your mercy is great," like David's "Be gracious to me, O God, as your loyal love is" (Psalm 51:1). The prayer offers no sacrifice and no promise of good works, only the confession and a vow to praise (1:15). Chronicles adds that after he returned Manasseh tore down the foreign gods and rebuilt the LORD's altar (2 Chronicles 33:15–16): the turning shows in deeds. The prayer and Chronicles together give both halves.

a: the whole army of the heavens
t: Claude's theory: the army Manasseh worshiped now sings to God
p: Manasseh bowed down to "all the army of the heavens." The prayer ends with that army praising God.
b: This is Claude's reading, offered as a possibility. The Greek hē dynamis tōn ouranōn, "the host (power) of the heavens," is the phrase the Greek Bible uses for the stars and heavenly beings. Chronicles' first charge against Manasseh is that "he bowed down to all the army of the heavens and served them" and built them altars in both courts of the LORD's house (2 Chronicles 33:3; 2 Chronicles 33:5). The prayer's last line reverses that worship: the whole army of the heavens, which the king served, is itself singing hymns to God, as in Nehemiah: "the army of the heavens bows low to you" (Nehemiah 9:6). The writer may have chosen the phrase for that reason. No commentator opened for this page says so.

a: yours is the glory forever. Amen.
p: A doxology, a short word of praise to close a prayer, like the ending later added to the Lord's Prayer.
b: Jewish and Christian prayers often end by giving glory to God. In the KJV, the Lord's Prayer in Matthew ends, "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen" (Matthew 6:13, KJV), an ending the oldest Greek manuscripts of Matthew lack. The prayer's own close, "yours is the glory forever," is the same kind of praise. Swete's notes show no difference between the manuscripts here. The KJV Apocrypha has "for ever and ever," a fuller English for the same Greek.
orig: σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. ἀμήν. (sou estin hē doxa eis tous aiōnas. amēn.)
